extracted.intended_audience: candidates preparing the French agrégation / ENS oral exams in mathematics (advanced undergraduates / graduate-level)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative expectations for delivering oral mathematics lessons for the agrégation (topics include representation theory on finite abelian groups, Fourier/DFT, rings Z/nZ, primes, finite fields, principal rings, series, field extensions, diophantine equations, etc.). Emphasises required theoretical facts, useful examples, applications and common pitfalls to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master representation theory and Fourier on finite abelian groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Be fully fluent with characters of finite abelian groups and the Fourier transform on such groups: definition of characters, irreducible characters (degree 1 in the abelian case), orthogonality relations, character tables, dual group, the Fourier transform as an algebra isomorphism, inversion and Plancherel formulas, convolution compatibility, and applications to discrete Fourier transform (DFT) and fast Fourier transform (FFT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: definition and properties of characters (Ulmer, Serre, Peyré references), decomposition into irreducibles (Maschke), orthogonality of characters and columns of character tables, proof that the dual pG forms an orthonormal basis of C rG s in the abelian case, Fourier transform is the unique extension of characters to the group algebra, Plancherel formula, compatibility with convolution (DFT is an algebra isomorphism). Applications: DFT/FFT complexity comparison, fast multiplication of polynomials and integers via interpolation at roots of unity (Cormen/Peyré), numerical PDEs and approximation of Fourier coefficients for heat equation solutions; mention also possible coding theory applications (Hadamard transform).

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the structure of Z/nZ (group and ring viewpoints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand Z/nZ as a group and as a ring: classes modulo n, cyclicity of Z/NZ, generators and calculation of φ(d), subgroups and quotients, and when Z/nZ is a field (n prime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be able to compute generators (a is generator iff a^n = 1), count generators via φ(d), know examples of roots of unity, describe subgroups and quotients, and understand consequences for multiplicative group of units. References: Risler, Colmez, Perrin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the Chinese remainder theorem (CRT) and generalisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the CRT statement, explicit isomorphism Z/nZ ≅ product of Z/pi^{αi}Z when applicable, and its use for solving congruences and decomposing rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit constructive isomorphism, counterexamples (e.g. Z/4Z), CRT for units (Z/nZ)ˆ and applications: multiplicativity of Euler's ϕ, studying p-adic components pZ/p^{α}Zˆ, and applications to solving congruences and decomposition used in algorithmic contexts. For advanced candidates, know the generalisation when moduli are not coprime (appearance of gcd and lcm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish group vs ring properties in Z/nZ and study automorphisms, nilpotents, idempotents
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting Z/nZ emphasise the difference between additive-group properties and ring-structure properties, and be able to characterise automorphisms, nilpotent and idempotent elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark explicitly which statements are about additive groups and which about rings; discuss automorphisms of Z/nZ, describe nilpotents and idempotents, and give examples. The jury expects clarity on this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include arithmetic applications and cryptography (RSA) when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrate the algebraic theory of Z/nZ by concrete arithmetic applications and cryptographic algorithms such as RSA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply CRT and group-of-units analysis to derive multiplicativity of Euler's function and to explain RSA principle (Gourdon, principle of RSA). Give diophantine applications and examples honouring classical arithmetic (e.g., Gauss).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare Dirichlet's theorem and a sketch of the prime number theorem (PNT)
rubrics_metrics.description: For lessons on primes, be prepared to state Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions and to outline the idea of the prime number theorem proof (analytic continuation of ζ, unique pole at 1, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury expects at least the statement of Dirichlet and the PNT and the idea of the PNT proof: study ζ(s), meromorphic continuation to Re(s)>0 with simple pole at 1, define auxiliary functions and bound their ratios to obtain the asymptotic. Mention consequences like infinitely many primes in specific congruence classes (e.g. 4m−1 forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain primality tests and Carmichael numbers; understand probabilistic tests and error bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Know simple non-primality tests (Fermat's test), the existence and properties of Carmichael numbers, and stronger tests such as Lehmer and Miller–Rabin with error probability estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give example Carmichael number 561 = 3·11·17, explain Fermat witness concept and why Fermat test is not an equivalence, present Miller–Rabin, note that if n composite then at least 3/4 of bases are witnesses (so N independent tests give error at most (1/4)^N).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand finite fields thoroughly (structure, Frobenius, automorphisms, primitive elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to state and use existence and uniqueness of finite fields F_{p^n}, describe their additive and multiplicative structures, subfields, Frobenius morphism and automorphism group, and the fact that F_{p^n}ˆ is cyclic (primitive element theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include: characteristic, prime subfield, dimension as vector space, uniqueness up to F_p-isomorphism, subfields correspond to divisors d|n (F_{p^d}), Frobenius automorphism and that Aut(F_{p^n}) is cyclic of order n. Apply to counting points and to cryptographic contexts when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomials irreducible: criteria over F_p, Z and Q; cyclotomic polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Know irreducibility criteria and examples: factorization of X^{p^n}-X over F_p, existence/count of irreducible polynomials of any degree, Eisenstein's criterion, reduction theorems, and properties/irreducibility of cyclotomic polynomials Φ_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be able to use factorization X^{p^n}-X, count irreducibles (formula with Möbius inversion), apply Eisenstein (examples), discuss counterexamples (e.g. X^4+1), state decomposition properties of Φ_n and irreducibility conditions mod p (when q generates (Z/nZ)ˆ). Give explicit worked examples (X^4−X, X^8−X, X^p−X−1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Give many concrete examples and linear-algebra applications in principal ideal domain (PID) lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid an overly theoretical presentation of PIDs: present classical examples beyond Z and K[X], illustrate algebraic consequences in linear algebra (e.g. minimal polynomial, diagonalization), and show how principal/factorial/euclidean properties relate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury expects numerous examples (decimals, Gauss/Eisenstein integers), explicit computation of irreducibles and units, mention minimal polynomial as an important application, possibly give examples of non-principal rings and diophantine applications. Warn against common misconceptions (e.g. erroneous claims about certain elements being irreducible/prime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat rings of integers in quadratic fields and units; apply to Pell's equation
rubrics_metrics.description: For quadratic integer rings, describe the ring of integers, conjugation, norm, classification of units (imaginary vs real quadratic fields) and apply these to equations like Pell's equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include examples: Gaussian and Eisenstein integers, characterize units and fundamental unit (example d=5), use to solve Pell for appropriate d (example d=3 with solution (2,1)), discuss when the ring is euclidean/principal and consequences for factorization and diophantine equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrate formal power series and generating functions with many examples and applications
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering formal series, emphasise examples and applications: generating functions in combinatorics, recurrence relations, partitions, Molien series for invariant theory, and operations on formal series (derivation, composition, inversion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury demands many examples: show how series compute Newton sums, count partitions, deduce recurrences (e.g. Fibonacci), explain P-recursive and Δ-finite series, and interpret Molien series (not just compute them). Discuss convergence/valuation/topology issues and substitution rules (careful with summability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Present field extension basics, telescoping basis theorem and constructive Galois ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover extensions of fields: definition, degree, algebraic vs transcendental elements, minimal polynomial, the tower (base télescopique) theorem and consequences for irreducibility, plus basic automorphism/Galois notions and constructibility applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit examples of adjoining roots, construction of splitting and decomposition fields, closure, mention finite fields as natural examples, apply to constructibility of regular polygons and use automorphisms to study Galois groups (monogenic extensions, Gal(Q(α)/Q) examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach diophantine equations starting from basic tools and methods (descent, modular reduction, rings of integers)
rubrics_metrics.description: For diophantine equations, present core techniques: Bézout and Gauss lemmas, solving linear diophantine equations, Smith normal form, Chinese remainder method, method of infinite descent, modular reduction arguments, use of arithmetic in rings of integers and factoriality considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work examples: ax+by=c solutions, multi-variable linear systems via Smith decomposition, parametric rational parametrisations (e.g. folium, conics), group law on curves, Pell and Mordell examples, applications of unique factorization (when available) and counterexamples. The jury expects concrete solved examples and emphasis on methods rather than pure theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical expectation: emphasise examples, applications and avoid purely abstract presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Across lessons, examiners expect candidates to prioritise worked examples, computational exercises and applications to demonstrate understanding and relevance rather than an excessively abstract development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple 'rapport du jury' remarks explicitly warn that candidates tend to be too theoretical; include illustrative computations, relate to applications (cryptography, numerical methods, representation tables), and when using advanced notions (Molien series, FFT) show interpretation on simple examples.
